vignette: The phone rings at 2:14 a.m. He answers, and the room narrows. His brother, Kahu, has been pulled under by a rip current off the northern coast. The dispatcher's voice is flat, procedural. By the time he reaches the shore, the salvage crew is already packing their ropes. Kahu's body is recovered, but the ocean leaves nothing behind, and the silence that follows is absolute. In the months that follow, the house grows heavy. He stops sleeping past midnight. Every storm front rolling in over the Pacific becomes a physical weight against his sternum. He finds himself standing at the edge of the driveway, not to garden or repair, but to watch the clouds, convinced that if he looks away, the sky will drop something else. He begins to measure his days in routines. He wakes at dawn, washes the same enamel mug three times, checks the gas stove, the windows, the deadbolt. When his wife asks him to stay present, to grieve with her instead of around her, he doesn't know how to translate grief into conversation. They drift apart quietly, then formally. The divorce papers sit on the counter like a settled matter, though neither of them ever really spoke about why they stopped speaking to each other. He turns to work. At fifty-five, he becomes a nanny, hired by a family who needs someone steady for their four-year-old daughter and six-year-old son. He arrives with a canvas bag of picture books, a first-aid kit he overpacks, and a quiet manner that puts children at ease. He knows exactly how to kneel to their level, how to hum low, rhythmic work songs from his childhood, how to notice when a small hand trembles or a breath hitches. But the work is laced with tension. When the children chase each other toward the street, his breath catches. He crosses the lawn before they reach the curb, his voice calm but firm: "Walk, tamariki. Always walk." He replays the sirens in his head when thunder rolls. He stops the weather app, avoids any story about coastal rescues, and sleeps with one ear toward the hallway. His shoulders remain perpetually drawn up, as if bracing for a strike that never comes, but always might. In my office, he sits with his hands folded over his knees, thumbs resting against each other like anchors. He speaks slowly, choosing words as if testing their weight. He describes waking at 3 a.m. to the sound of his own pulse, then lying still, listening for the drip of a tap that isn't there. He talks about teaching the children how to tie their shoes, how to share, how to ask for help, while internally rehearsing exactly what he would do if they vanished from the backyard. He laughs sometimes, a dry, startled sound, then stops himself, as if amused by his own presence in the room. He doesn't avoid talking about Kahu, but when the name comes up, his jaw tightens, his gaze drifts toward the window, and the silence stretches until he decides it's safe to continue. He arrives early to sessions, always. He leaves precisely on time, checking his phone once, then twice, as if confirming the world has held together while he was here. He waters the office ferns without being asked. He remembers the name of the child he watches on the street corner, asking after them with a quiet, practiced warmth that masks the vigilance humming just beneath it. He walks back to his car slowly, scanning the street, the sky, the faces passing by, carrying the weight of a loss that settled in his bones and refuses to dissolve. The morning air is cool. He gets in, starts the engine, and waits for the familiar, quiet tension to settle before driving home.
